about.title: San Juan Capistrano Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: San Juan Capistrano's mix of local streets and busy through-routes creates a steady flow of traffic, and with it, collisions. Public records show 141 injury crashes and 171 injured people in the most recent reporting year, with Fridays between 3 and 5 p.m. seeing a noticeable spike. Corridors like I-5, Camino Capistrano, Ortega Highway, and Del Obispo Street carry heavy volume, and a moment's distraction there can change your week or your year. If you were injured, what happens in the first days matters — insurers move fast, and evidence like skid marks, dashcam footage, or witness memory fades quickly. LawProactive isn't a law firm; we're a free service that connects you with an independent personal injury attorney who can evaluate your situation, explain your options under California law, and work on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless you recover. Let someone who understands local roads and California claims help you sort through what comes next.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Before Talking to the Insurer

items.title: California's Fault Rules Can Work Against You
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so an insurer may try to pin partial blame on you to reduce what you're owed. An attorney can push back on unfair fault allocations before they become part of your file.

items.title: The Clock Is Shorter Than You Think
items.desc: California generally gives you two years to file a car accident claim, but if a government entity was involved — say, a poorly maintained road — that window can shrink to as little as six months. Missing it can end your case before it starts.

items.title: Recorded Statements Can Backfire
items.desc: The other driver's insurer may ask for a recorded statement early, hoping you'll say something that limits your claim. An attorney can handle that communication so your words aren't used against you later.

items.question: How long do I have to file a claim after a crash in San Juan Capistrano?
items.answer: In most cases, California law gives you two years from the date of the crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. If your accident involved a government-owned road or vehicle, that deadline can be much shorter — sometimes just six months. It's best to talk with an attorney soon after the crash so you don't lose your options.

items.question: Should I give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company?
items.answer: You're generally not required to, and it's often better not to without speaking to an attorney first. Insurers sometimes use recorded statements to find reasons to reduce or deny a claim. An independent attorney connected through LawProactive can advise you on how to respond.

items.question: I was partly at fault for a crash near Ortega Highway — can I still recover damages?
items.answer: Possibly, yes. California follows a pure comparative fault rule, which means you can still recover compensation even if you share some blame, though your recovery may be reduced by your percentage of fault. An attorney can help make sure fault isn't overstated against you.
